text:
[Does It Look Sequential? (RecSys 2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.12008v1) evaluates sequential structure across 15 datasets using interaction shuffling, including inference-only perturbations of fixed GRU4Rec and SASRec models. It measures accuracy degradation and top-K Jaccard overlap. Several datasets show weak sequential structure. However, full-history shuffling changes both the last item and earlier ordering, so its effect cannot isolate immediate-predecessor dependence.

[Residual Dominance (2026)](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.14021v1) provides a more targeted control: compare original histories, prefix shuffling with the final item fixed, and full shuffling. SASRec often shows much smaller degradation when the final item is preserved; GRU4Rec exhibits weaker contrasts. This supports testing last-position sensitivity explicitly, but the paper’s Transformer residual mechanism should not be assumed to explain GRU behavior. Prefix-shuffle robustness also does not exclude dependence on unordered prefix content.

Recommended GRU4Rec diagnostic design, extending these controls: compare last-item-only input and progressively longer recent suffixes; remove equal numbers of recent versus randomly selected earlier items while always preserving the final item; separately delete the final item versus one earlier item. Keep retained-item order, left padding, final-nonpadding readout, validation users, targets and candidates fixed. Repeat random perturbations and report paired uncertainty using the same checkpoint. Greater damage from recent-history removal alone establishes sensitivity to broader recent context, not a last-item shortcut—especially when that removal includes the final item. These are inference sensitivity probes, not proof of causal reliance or dataset-wide absence of sequential signal.
